colorado.citation: HB25-1090, "Protections Against Deceptive Pricing Practices" (codified as amendments to the Colorado Consumer Protection Act, C.R.S. Title 6, Art. 1, and to landlord-tenant law, C.R.S. Title 38, Art. 12)
colorado.requires: Landlords/rental companies must clearly and conspicuously disclose the 'total price' of a residential rental as a single, prominent number (in larger/more prominent font than any component figure), before a prospective tenant applies. The total price must include all mandatory recurring fees and charges except: (a) government taxes/charges, and (b) actual utility costs billed directly by a third-party utility provider (which may be itemized separately if properly disclosed). The bill also PROHIBITS landlords from charging certain fees outright, including charges for common-area utilities, pest control, and property taxes, and caps increases on other mandatory (non-utility) fees during a lease term of one year or less. This is the likely statutory driver of the 'Total Monthly Leasing Price' + itemized fee schedule with a 'Date of Issuance' seen on CO apartment marketing sites, since the CO Attorney General's guidance (Dec 2025) calls for a clear total-price figure and itemized, dated fee disclosures. Signed April 21, 2025 by Gov. Polis; prime sponsors Reps. Emily Sirota & Naquetta Ricks, Sens. Mike Weissman & Lisa Cutter.
colorado.applies_to: Landlords and rental companies advertising or leasing residential property in Colorado (broad consumer-pricing-transparency bill that also covers non-housing goods/services, with carve-outs for food service, broadband/cable providers, and delivery network companies meeting compliance standards).
colorado.enforcement: Violation is a deceptive/unconscionable trade practice under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act (C.R.S. § 6-1-105 et seq.). Tenants can send a written demand for a refund of unlawfully collected fees; if the landlord does not refund within 14 days, the landlord is liable for actual damages plus 18% annual compounding interest (some secondary sources describe added treble-damages exposure under CCPA's general private-right-of-action provisions). The Colorado Attorney General may adopt implementing rules and may bring enforcement actions (the AG already partnered with the FTC on the Greystar case, see federal section).

colorado.citation: HB24-1057, "Prohibit Algorithmic Devices Used for Rent Setting" (2024) - DID NOT PASS
colorado.requires: Would have prohibited landlords from using algorithmic devices to set rent, specifically devices trained on or incorporating nonpublic competitor data; would have made violations an unfair/deceptive trade practice under the CCPA. Passed the House 45-19 (March 4, 2024) but died in the Senate (Senate receded from amendments 17-18, May 1, 2024).
colorado.applies_to: Would have applied to landlords setting rent for residential premises.

colorado.citation: HB25-1004 (2025 successor bill banning algorithmic rent-setting 'coordinators') - PASSED LEGISLATURE, VETOED BY GOVERNOR
colorado.effective: N/A - vetoed May 2025, never took effect
colorado.requires: Would have banned landlords from using AI/algorithmic 'coordinator' software/data-analytics services that perform a rent-coordinating function across multiple landlords (aimed at RealPage-style revenue management tools). Passed the General Assembly along party lines.
colorado.applies_to: Would have applied to landlords and algorithmic pricing/coordination service providers.
colorado.enforcement: N/A - Governor Jared Polis vetoed the bill in May 2025, reasoning that such price-fixing conduct is already illegal under the Colorado Antitrust Act and that removing the software could eliminate a tool with legitimate vacancy-management uses.

colorado.citation: FTC & State of Colorado v. Greystar Real Estate Partners, LLC - stipulated settlement/order
colorado.requires: Greystar must clearly and prominently disclose the total monthly price of a rental unit (including all mandatory fees) whenever it advertises or quotes rental prices; must pay $24 million total ($23M to FTC, $1M to Colorado) for allegedly advertising an attractive base rent while not disclosing mandatory recurring fees (tech, trash, package concierge, pest control, utility admin, amenities) until late in the application/leasing process, often after a non-refundable application fee was paid.
colorado.applies_to: Greystar Real Estate Partners specifically (a major national multifamily operator/manager with a large Colorado/Denver-metro presence); the case is illustrative of the FTC's and Colorado AG's joint enforcement approach to rental fee transparency, using existing Section 5 FTC Act / CCPA authority even before HB25-1090's 2026 effective date.
colorado.enforcement: Joint FTC (Section 5, FTC Act) and Colorado Attorney General (CCPA) enforcement action resulting in a stipulated court judgment/order.

federal.action: Trade Regulation Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees ("Junk Fees Rule"), 16 C.F.R. Part 464
federal.issued: 2024-12 (announced Dec 2024); published in Federal Register early January 2025
federal.effective: 2025-05 (approximately 120 days after Federal Register publication; commonly cited as effective in May 2025)
federal.scope: COVERS ONLY live-event ticketing and short-term lodging (hotels, motels, inns, short-term/vacation rentals). The FTC's original 2023 proposal was broader ('a wide range of businesses'), but the FINAL rule was explicitly narrowed and EXCLUDES long-term residential rental housing, financial services, and corporate housing arrangements. Requires covered businesses to display the total price (including all mandatory fees) as the most prominent figure in any advertisement, and prohibits misrepresenting the nature/purpose/refundability of fees.

federal.action: Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) on Unfair or Deceptive Rental Housing Fee Practices
federal.status: ANPRM (preliminary rulemaking stage - NOT a proposed or final rule yet)
federal.issued: Draft ANPRM submitted to OMB/OIRA for review in January 2026; ANPRM published in Federal Register March 12-13, 2026
federal.effective: Not yet effective - this is a fact-finding/comment stage. Public comment period ran roughly March-April 2026 (comment deadline cited as April 13, 2026).
federal.scope: This is a SEPARATE rulemaking track specifically targeting long-term residential rental housing fee practices - the category explicitly excluded from the Dec 2024 final Junk Fees Rule. The 74-question ANPRM covers: total-rent disclosure clarity, fee/charge transparency (nature, amount, refundability), application fee practices, security deposit handling, utility billing and government-fee passthroughs, and other leasing/payment practices. It does not appear to include a carve-out for affordable housing providers. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson directed staff to begin this rulemaking following the Greystar settlement.
federal.confidence: verified - direct fetch of federalregister.gov page was blocked (403/redirect), so scope/date details are drawn from secondary legal-analysis sources (Katten, Inside Privacy, GT Law) that cite the Federal Register notice; the underlying existence and March 2026 timing of the ANPRM is corroborated across multiple independent sources including FTC's own press release title.

federal.action: Fact sheet: 'Biden-Harris Administration Takes on Junk Fees in Rental Housing to Lower Costs for Renters'
federal.status: Policy announcement / voluntary private-sector commitments (not regulation)
federal.scope: Announced that Zillow, Apartments.com, and AffordableHousing.com made VOLUNTARY commitments to provide consumers with total, upfront cost information on rental listings (rather than surprise fees revealed later in the process). HUD simultaneously released research on rental junk fees as a blueprint for a nationwide effort, and the administration highlighted state legislative activity (citing states 'from Connecticut to California').

other_states.citation: Minn. Stat. § 504B.120 (created by 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 52, art. 19, § 84)
other_states.requires: Landlord must disclose all nonoptional fees in the lease agreement; the sum of rent + all nonoptional fees must be labeled the 'Total Monthly Payment' and listed on the first page of the lease. Nonoptional fees must also be disclosed in unit advertisements, and ads/leases must specify whether utilities are included in rent. Violations carry treble-damages liability and potential attorney-fee awards to tenants.

other_states.state: Minnesota (general consumer/'junk fees' law, broader than housing)
other_states.citation: Minnesota HF 3438 (2024) - amends Minn. Stat. Ch. 325F consumer protection provisions
other_states.requires: General state ban on 'junk fees' - businesses must incorporate all mandatory fees into advertised prices (any fee needed to complete a purchase, or that a reasonable consumer would expect to be included). Excludes taxes and shipping from the required total.
other_states.applies_to: Businesses generally (not housing-specific, but applies to landlords as businesses).

other_states.citation: SB 478 (2023), the 'Honest Pricing Law' - amends the Consumers Legal Remedies Act (Cal. Civ. Code § 1770)
other_states.requires: Prohibits advertising a price that excludes mandatory fees (a 'drip pricing' ban); the advertised price must include all fees/charges except government taxes and shipping. Applies broadly to goods/services including short-term lodging and, per CA DOJ/AG FAQ and law-firm analysis, residential rental listings.
other_states.applies_to: Businesses offering goods/services to CA consumers, including landlords advertising rental housing.

other_states.citation: SB 611 (2024), 'Residential rental properties: fees and security'
other_states.effective: 2025-04-01 (fee/deposit provisions); rental-advertising provisions cited by some secondary sources as effective July 2025

other_states.effective: 2025-09-02 (AG regulation); a related legislative provision is cited with an effective date of 2026-07-01

other_states.applies_to: Businesses operating in Massachusetts, including residential landlords.

other_states.citation: Local Law 119 of 2024, the FARE Act ('Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses Act')
other_states.requires: Whoever hires a real estate broker (not the tenant, unless the tenant hired the broker) is responsible for the broker's fee. Before lease execution, landlords must provide tenants a signed, itemized written disclosure of all fees payable to the landlord, retained for 3 years with a copy given to the tenant. This is a broker-fee-allocation and itemized-fee-disclosure law, not a 'single total price in advertising' law like Colorado/Minnesota/Massachusetts.

other_states.enforcement: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP).

lease_term_disclosure.detail: No law or regulation was found in this research that requires a landlord, revenue-management vendor, or advertising platform to disclose WHICH lease term (e.g., 2-month vs. 15-month) an advertised or quoted rent applies to, nor any requirement to disclose that a displayed price is generated by algorithmic/dynamic-pricing software. This appears to be a genuine regulatory gap, as the user suspected. What DOES exist, and is adjacent but distinct: (1) Colorado's HB25-1090 (effective Jan 1, 2026) requires a single 'total price' disclosure and caps mandatory-fee increases during a lease term of one year or less, but does not require disclosing that base rent varies by lease length or showing rents for alternative lease terms side by side. (2) Massachusetts' 940 CMR 38.00 (effective Sept 2, 2025) requires disclosing the LEASE TYPE (month-to-month, 12-month, auto-renewing 12-month) but not that the quoted price is specific to one lease-length option among several priced differently. (3) A wave of city ordinances - San Francisco (Sec. 37.10C of the Rent Ordinance, effective Oct 14, 2024), Philadelphia (Bill No. 240823, Oct 2024), Berkeley, Minneapolis, San Diego, Jersey City NJ, Providence RI, Hoboken NJ (2025) - BAN the use of algorithmic rent-setting/revenue-management devices built on nonpublic competitor data, but these are prohibitions on the software, not consumer-facing disclosure mandates about how a quoted price was generated or which lease term it reflects. (4) Colorado twice tried and failed to enact a state-level algorithmic-pricing ban: HB24-1057 (died in Senate, May 2024) and HB25-1004 (passed the legislature but vetoed by Gov. Polis, May 2025, on the rationale that such conduct is already actionable under the Colorado Antitrust Act). Neither bill, even had it passed, would have created a consumer disclosure requirement - both were use-bans, not disclosure regimes. (5) The DOJ's Nov 24, 2025 proposed consent decree settling United States v. RealPage (joined by 10 states including Colorado) restricts RealPage's use of nonpublic/active-lease data and requires data to be at least 12 months old before use in model training (implicitly acknowledging the ~12-month/annual-lease norm), and imposes a court-approved monitor - but this is a data-use and antitrust remedy, not a tenant-facing disclosure obligation about term-based price variation. No provision found in the settlement, the DOJ complaint summaries, or law-firm analyses of it that requires disclosing to consumers that pricing varies by lease term.

notes: Could NOT verify: (1) 'HB24-1090' as named by the user does not exist in Colorado's bill-numbering system for that biennium in a form matching the described law; the actual, verified bill is HB25-1090 (introduced/passed in the 2025 session, effective Jan 1, 2026). The user's instinct about the substance was correct but the bill number/year was not - flag this clearly to the user. (2) The exact composition of the FTC's rental-housing ANPRM (comment period start/end dates, full question list) is drawn from secondary legal-alert sources because the primary federalregister.gov and ftc.gov URLs returned redirects/403 errors to this research tool; the underlying facts (ANPRM exists, targets long-term rental housing, follows the Greystar settlement, ~March 2026 timing) were corroborated across 3+ independent secondary sources so confidence is reasonably high, but a direct read of the Federal Register notice or FTC press release is recommended before citing exact dates/question counts in any external-facing material. (3) Minnesota's general 'junk fees' bill number (HF 3438) and Oregon's HB 3521 citation were each corroborated by only a single secondary source and should be independently double-checked against the MN Legislature and Oregon Legislative Information System (OLIS) respectively before being treated as fully verified. (4) No Denver- or Boulder-specific municipal total-price/fee-disclosure ordinance was found; this is reported as a negative finding, not an exhaustive one - direct review of the Denver Revised Municipal Code and Boulder Municipal Code was not performed. (5) No CFPB or FHFA rulemaking specific to rental fee/total-price disclosure was found; CFPB's role has been limited to a 2023 joint RFI with the FTC on tenant screening. (6) Confirmed there is NO disclosure requirement anywhere in current law (state, local, or federal, proposed or enacted) tied to lease-TERM-based price variation or to algorithmic/dynamic pricing methodology - existing and proposed measures either ban the software (several cities) or mandate a single all-in total price (CO, MN, MA, CA) without addressing why/how the underlying base rent number was set or whether it varies by lease length. This is the clearest confirmed gap relevant to the navigator tool's stated concern about $4,133 (2-month) vs $1,552 (15-month) pricing for the same unit.
